title: Mirabel and the Smile
premise: Casper Winterbourne, a late-night radio host, begins receiving calls from listeners who died the previous week — and the calls are coming from inside the house. When their childhood imaginary friend, Mirabel, appears on the porch unchanged after thirty years, Casper learns the entity was never a friend but a witness, bound to the house by a contract signed by the last living resident. To survive until sunrise, Casper must uncover what their late grandmother invited in decades ago and reach the dying last resident, Mr. Alder Voss, before he signs the house over to a developer — an act that would transfer the invitation to a new, unprotected owner. In the end, Casper burns the original deed at dawn, freeing Mirabel, who is revealed to be the ghost of the grandmother's first victim, and Casper signs nothing, walking out of the house as the sun rises and the voices finally go silent.
about_author: Astrid Quintana is a former night-shift dispatcher from coastal Maine who claims she wrote her first ghost story during a blackout that lasted three days. She lives in a house she refuses to describe, with a dog named Omen and a standing rule never to answer the phone after 3 a.m.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. During a routine late-night broadcast, a caller describes her own funeral in perfect detail; Casper assumes a prank until the obituary checks out. The emotional beat is unease — the professional skeptic's first hairline crack, played out on air while the switchboard lights up with numbers that shouldn't exist.

chapters.title: The Switchboard
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Three more calls from the recently dead, each mentioning 'the house on Fenwick Lane' — Casper's childhood address. Studio equipment fails in patterns too deliberate for coincidence. The beat is mounting dread disguised as journalistic curiosity.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Remember
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper drives to Fenwick Lane, finding the house intact but wrong — mail addressed to the grandmother, dead eleven years. A neighbor mentions 'the girl on the porch' who's been there 'as long as anyone recalls.' The beat is the uncanny intrusion into the familiar.

chapters.title: Mirabel
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. On the porch sits Mirabel — the imaginary friend, ageless, smiling, unchanged since Casper was seven. She speaks in Casper's own childhood voice and says, 'You came back to sign.' The beat is vertigo: comfort curdling into recognition that the imaginary was never imaginary.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, with flashbacks. Casper reviews the noises, the cold spots, the whispers rationalized across seven years of ownership, realizing each 'explanation' was a mercy the house granted. The beat is self-reckoning — the skeptic discovering they've been complicit in their own deception.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper finds Alder Voss, 94, in a care facility, holding the deed to Fenwick Lane and a developer's contract. Voss mistakes Casper for someone named 'Edda' and begs forgiveness. The beat is the first hard clue: the house's fate hinges on a signature.

chapters.title: Edda's Ledger
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, intercut with 1968 diary entries from grandmother Edda. The ledger records payments made in 'teeth, time, and names' to something she called the Tenant. The beat is horrified inheritance — Casper learning their bloodline holds the lease on the horror.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Back on air, Casper asks listeners if anyone else has seen Mirabel; a caller who died in 1974 answers, describing the same smile. The station manager threatens to fire Casper. The beat is isolation — the truth-teller disbelieved by the living and heard only by the dead.

chapters.title: The Terms
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, rendered in eerie second person. She explains the contract: the house must always have a resident who has been 'invited,' and when Voss signs, the invitation passes to whoever holds the deed. The beat is cold clarity — the rules of the trap, finally legible.

chapters.title: First Night
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper locks themselves inside the house to search for the original deed before Voss can sign at week's end. The walls breathe; the dead call from every room. The beat is siege — committing to the fight and immediately regretting the ground chosen.

chapters.title: The Room That Isn't
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Behind the pantry, a door that appears only after midnight opens onto a nursery where children's voices count to sunrise. Casper finds a child's drawing of Edda shaking hands with something tall. The beat is dread deepening into evidence.

chapters.title: Developer's Son
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The developer's son, Marcus Hale, arrives to prep the sale and is nearly taken by the house, which wants a new resident immediately. Casper saves him and gains an unlikely ally. The beat is reluctant alliance — two people who should be enemies bound by survival.

chapters.title: What Mirabel Was
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She remembers being a girl named Wren, the Tenant's first payment in 1911, kept smiling so the house would have a face the living could love. The beat is tragic revelation — the monster's mask is a victim's face.

chapters.title: The Care Facility at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: Casper and Marcus's POV, alternating. They reach Voss, but the Tenant's influence has spread — staff walk in loops, and Voss's signature is already half-written in blood. The beat is a race against a clock that is also a person.

chapters.title: Voss's Confession
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. He reveals he was Edda's accomplice, that the 'invitations' were lures for the desperate, and that he signed once before — and un-signed it by never leaving. The beat is the banality of complicity; the villain is an old man's cowardice.

chapters.title: The House Objects
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Driving back, the house pulls at Casper from miles away — radio stations bleed into one voice, roads loop toward Fenwick Lane. The beat is the trap tightening: the house will not permit its lease to be broken from outside.

chapters.title: Invited
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The Tenant, speaking through every dead caller at once, offers Casper the deal Edda took: safety, the show's success, forever — in exchange for becoming the next resident who invites. The beat is temptation at its most reasonable.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. On air, at 3:33 a.m., Casper publicly refuses the deal and names the dead callers one by one, restoring their names to them — an act outside any law, which the contract never anticipated. The beat is defiance as weapon.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Casper and Mirabel's POV. They find the original deed hidden in the nursery's walls; burning it requires it be done by someone 'invited who was never paid' — Mirabel. But she can only touch it if someone speaks her true name: Wren. The beat is the cost of survival made literal.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Climax. Casper speaks Wren's name; she takes the burning deed into her hands as the Tenant tears through the house, wearing every face it has collected. Voss dies signing a renunciation scrawled in ash. The beat is sacrifice, terror, and the fire holding.

chapters.title: The Last Call
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Dawn. The house is empty and ordinary; Mirabel/Wren is gone, leaving only the child's drawing, now showing a girl walking out a door. The final caller thanks Casper and hangs up forever. The beat is grief braided with release.

chapters.title: Off the Air
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, epilogue. Casper signs nothing, sells the lot to Marcus as undeveloped land, and ends the show with a final broadcast about the names of the forgotten. On a new porch, in a new town, a child waves at someone unseen — and Casper, watching, smiles and does not look away. The beat is identity remade: the survivor who chose witness over safety.
